'
Vacuum

Without a material medium sound does not travel: there is no speed or wavelength.

'
lit.'<p>Al chocar con una superficie el soni:
'

When sound hits a surface it is reflected. If the obstacle is far away we hear an echo: the pulse travels there and back, so the distance is d = v·t/2. With a wall 170 m away, the echo returns in 1 s. Bats, dolphins and ship sonar use echoes to locate objects.

'
lit.'<p>El <b>oído externo</b> conduce la on:
'

The outer ear channels the wave to the eardrum, which vibrates. The ossicles (hammer, anvil and stirrup) amplify the vibration and pass it to the cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve impulses: the base responds to high pitches and the apex to low ones. Each species hears a different range (graph «Hearing ranges»).

'
lit.'<p>El parlante vibra y empuja las partí:
'

The speaker vibrates and pushes the air particles, which in turn push their neighbours: compressions (particles close together) and rarefactions (spread apart) travel outwards. It is a longitudinal wave: the particles oscillate in the same direction the wave travels, but they do not move along with it; what travels is energy. In a vacuum there are no particles and sound does not travel.

'
lit.'<p>La <b>amplitud</b> es cuánto se alej:
'

Amplitude is how far the particles move from their rest position. The greater the amplitude, the more energy the wave carries and the more intense (louder) the sound. Intensity is measured in decibels (dB): a conversation is ≈ 60 dB and sustained levels above 85 dB damage hearing.

'
lit.'<p>La <b>frecuencia</b> f es el número:
'

Frequency f is the number of oscillations per second, in hertz (Hz). Low frequencies sound deep and high ones shrill. The human ear hears roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; below are infrasounds and above are ultrasounds, used by bats, dolphins and ultrasound scans.

'
lit.'<p>La <b>longitud de onda</b> λ es la d:
'

The wavelength λ is the distance between two compressions. It satisfies v = λ·f. Speed depends on the medium: ≈ 343 m/s in air, ≈ 1480 m/s in water and ≈ 5960 m/s in steel, because in solids and liquids the particles are more tightly bound. With a higher speed, the same frequency has a longer λ.

'
